trends.intro: Hair searches rising on Pinterest right now. These are the words clients search with, so using them in captions and on-screen text can help your posts show up when they look.

source.name: Pinterest Trends, US, data through Nov 6, 2026

groups.label: Shades and tones, up from last year

trends.takeaway: Softer, darker, lower-maintenance color is climbing into winter.

ideas.title: Your unpopular opinion
ideas.principle: People like it when someone says what they really think. If they agree, they feel understood. So they like it and share it.
dissection: The hook
A mic held up to a stylist. One question on screen: "What's your unpopular hair opinion?" You want to hear her answer before she says it. That's curiosity.
What they did

Lots of short opinions, one or two sentences each. Like "Bangs aren't for everyone" and "Short hair isn't less work." Big words pop up as they talk, with a small photo for each point. The spot keeps changing too: cutting, washing, stocking shelves.
Why people kept watching
Every opinion is something clients believe and stylists have feelings about. Each new answer starts the curiosity over: what will the next one be?
Why people liked and shared it
Agreement. The top comment says the short hair one is so true, and over 1,000 people liked that comment. When we agree, we feel understood. That's why people liked it and sent it to friends.
ideas.concept: Share a hair opinion you really believe. Pick one you've seen with your own clients. Talk about hair, not other stylists.
ideas.hook: What's my unpopular hair opinion? Short hair is more work than long hair.
ideas.hook2: Three hair opinions I'll stand behind, even if you won't like them.
steps: Write down 3 opinions. Add one reason for each, like "Blunt bangs can make you look older."
Hold your phone at eye level. Put the question on screen. Answer each one fast.
Caption: "Agree or disagree?" Answer the first comments, even the ones that disagree. Don't argue.

ref.headline: A salon team, one mic, one question
ref.desc: A salon asked its stylists one question: "What's your unpopular hair opinion?" Each one answered. About 50 seconds.

shots: Solo: you at your station, eye level, one take per clip
Team: someone off camera holds the phone or a mic up to each stylist in turn
Optional: a photo for each point (the bang, the bob) dropped in the corner
structure: Take two, take three (one breath each)
talking: One sentence for the opinion, one for the reason
Say it like you'd say it to a client, not like a lecture
No digs at other stylists, salons or clients
guide.caption: "Agree or disagree?" plus the take you'd defend hardest. Reply to disagreement with your reason, not an argument.
adapt: Blonding: "Toning every visit isn't always needed"
Cutting: "Face-framing layers aren't for every face"
Salon owner: ask each stylist on your team the question

ideas.title: Raw lift
ideas.principle: Show a step most stylists hide, and say what it tells you. Honest work, explained, is what people trust.
dissection: The hook
Foils come off one after another at the bowl, filmed from above. Foil pulls are satisfying to watch. Your eyes want to see the next one.
What they did
Foils out. A slow brush through the wet, raw blonde. Then a jump to the finished hair at 16 seconds. Under 20 seconds total.
What made it different
Surprise. The caption said the foil work was so good, they left it as raw lift with no toner. Most stylists wouldn't even show hair before toner, let alone leave it.
Why it beat her usual
About 27 times her normal views. You get the satisfying part and a gorgeous finished blonde, with no toner at all. People can see the work is real and holds up.
ideas.concept: Film the hair right out of the foils. Say what you see. Is it even? Does it need toner? Say why.
ideas.hook: Straight out of the foils. No toner yet. Here's what I'm looking at.
ideas.hook2: This is the part most stylists never post.
steps: Hold your phone above the bowl. Film the foils coming out for 5 seconds.
Brush slowly. Say one thing you see, like "It's even from root to end."
Show the finished hair for 3 seconds. Caption: what you wanted at this step.

ref.headline: Foils out, raw blonde, no toner
ref.desc: A blonde stylist took the foils out, brushed the hair, then showed the finished hair. Under 20 seconds.

shots: Overhead at the bowl, foils coming out
A slow brush-through along the part
structure: Brush-through + one line of what you see (5–15s)
talking: Say what you see in plain words: "even lift, no hot roots"
If it needs toner, say why; that's the insight
Don't call it perfect; show it
guide.caption: One line on what the raw stage told you, then the gloss or toner you chose (or didn't).
adapt: Brunette lightening: show the raw level before the gloss and why you're keeping warmth
Gray blending: the lift on the gray before blending
Lived-in blonde: how your teasing shows up in the raw lift

ideas.title: Real hair only
ideas.principle: Say out loud something every stylist is feeling. Then answer it with your real work. People share what they've felt too.
dissection: The hook
The caption names something every stylist has felt lately: clients bringing inspo photos that are fake AI. It's relatable right away.
What they did
Photos of one real client's bobs over several years. Beautiful work, and the point is that every photo is real.
Why it worked
It's relatable. Stylists commented that they can't find real inspo either. The idea is what makes the post work, not fancy photos.
Good to know
The numbers are small for a photo post, about 2 times her usual likes. It's here for the idea. It's timely, and every stylist can do it.
ideas.concept: Post a real client's hair in daylight. Say it's real. Say how long it lasts between visits.
ideas.hook: Half the inspo photos I get now are AI. This is real hair, on a real client.
ideas.hook2: Bring me this one. It's a real person, and I can actually do it.
steps: Take photos of a client by a window. Get 2 or 3 sides. No filters.
First photo: your best one. Add the words "real client, no filter."
Last photo: how many weeks between visits, and how long it takes to style.

ref.headline: Real photos in an AI-inspo world
ref.desc: A colorist posted real photos of one client's hair over the years. The caption talked about fake AI inspo photos.
ref.numbers: About 2 times her usual likes for a photo post

shots: Front, side and back in daylight
Optional: the same client a few months later, if you have it
structure: Slide 1: best photo + "real client, no filter"
Last slide: upkeep in two lines
talking: Say it in first person: "the inspo I get", not "you should"
No dig at AI users; just show what's real
guide.caption: Your line about AI inspo, then one sentence on what this hair takes to maintain. Invite clients to save it for their consult.
adapt: Blonding: a real lived-in blonde at week 8, not just day one
Cutting: the same cut at 6 weeks
Extensions: how they look after a month of real life

ideas.title: Wet vs dry
ideas.principle: Show the moment that worries clients, then the moment that makes them feel better. Wanting to see the "after" keeps people watching.
dissection: The hook
Wet hair being combed with "Wet" on screen. It looks dark and flat. That's exactly what makes clients panic at the bowl.
What they did
6 seconds wet. Then a jump to the same client, dry and styled, with "Dry" on screen. It's much lighter and brighter. 15 seconds, no talking.
Why people kept watching
Anticipation. You want to see how light it really dries. The jump from dark to bright is the reward for waiting.
Why it beat her usual
Several times her normal views, and over 10K likes. It answers a question every color client has. Useful posts get saved and sent.
ideas.concept: Film the same hair two times. First wet at the bowl. Then dry at the mirror. Film the same side both times.
ideas.hook: Wet vs dry. Don't panic at the bowl.
ideas.hook2: This is why I tell you not to judge it wet.
steps: After toning, comb the hair flat. Film 5 seconds from the side. Add the word "Wet."
After styling, film the same side for 5 seconds. Add the word "Dry."
Caption: water makes color look darker. That's normal.

ref.headline: Wet, then dry
ref.desc: The same client, wet at the bowl, then dry. Each part has a label. 15 seconds. No talking.

shots: Side view at the bowl, hair combed flat, wet
Same side, same distance, dry and styled, a little movement
talking: If you add text, keep it to the two labels and one reassuring line
guide.caption: "Wet = darker, dry = lighter" in your own words, plus one line for clients who panic at the bowl.
adapt: Brunette: wet looks almost black, dry shows the dimension
Copper: wet reads deeper and redder, dry shows the true tone
Extensions: wet shows the blend lines, dry shows how they disappear
Gray blending: wet looks flat, dry shows the soft blend

ideas.title: Hair I did today (with prices)
ideas.principle: People are nosy about what things cost. Showing your real day, with real prices, answers a question everyone wants answered.
dissection: The hook
The stylist on camera with the title "Hair I did today as a lived-in color specialist (with prices)." You stay to see the prices. That's curiosity.
What they did
Each client's finished hair, one after another. Each one shows the client number, the service and the price. About 30 seconds.
Why people kept watching
People are curious about prices and what a stylist really does all day. Each new client starts the curiosity over: what's next, and what did it cost?
Why it works for everyone
Lots of stylists post this kind of video. But every stylist's day is different, so every version is different.
ideas.concept: At the end of your day, show each client's hair. Add the service and the price.
ideas.hook: Hair I did today as a [your specialty], with prices.
ideas.hook2: What a Tuesday behind the chair actually looks like, prices included.
steps: Film each client's finished hair for 3 or 4 seconds.
Start with you on camera for 3 seconds. Put the title on screen.
Show each client with the service and price. End with: "Which one is your favorite?"

ref.headline: Today's clients, with prices
ref.desc: A color stylist showed every client from one day. Each one had the service and the price.
ref.numbers: 200K+ views · about 3 to 4 times her usual

shots: Each client's finished hair, 3–4 seconds each, same spot and light if you can
talking: Let the labels talk; no voiceover needed
Use the service names clients would actually book
guide.caption: Your specialty, your city, and an invitation to book. Prices match your menu.
adapt: Cutting: "cuts I did today, with prices"
Extensions: method, rows and price per client
Newer stylists: "what I charge at year two" builds trust too
